title: Origin of the Ahoms
body: Early in the thirteenth century, a band of hardy hill men known as the Ahoms wandered into the eastern extremity of the Brahmaputra valley. They were an offshoot of the great Tai or Shan race occupying Upper Burma and Western Yunnan. Their descendants eventually brought the whole Brahmaputra valley under their rule and limited the eastward extension of the Mughal empire.
key_facts: Arrived in the eastern Brahmaputra valley early in the thirteenth century
Offshoot of the Tai or Shan race from Upper Burma and Western Yunnan

subject: Assam History
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 70

title: Ahom Buranjis
body: The Ahoms possessed a well-developed historic sense and maintained chronicles called Buranjis. These texts were written up by priests and nobles from time to time, providing a careful, reliable, and continuous narrative of Ahom rule, which serves as the primary source for their history.
key_facts: Ahom chronicles are known as Buranjis
Maintained by priests and nobles to record continuous narratives of rule
image_query: Assamese manuscript Buranji
subject: Assam History
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 70

title: Ahom Legend of the Flood
body: Ahom traditions include a legend of a great flood caused by intense solar heat that cracked the earth and released boiling water. An old man named Thaolipling and a cow survived in a stone boat on a northern mountain. After a great fire, a surviving pumpkin branch produced a giant gourd containing all living creatures, which was eventually split open by Indra's son Aiphalan.
key_facts: Thaolipling and a cow survived the flood in a stone boat
A giant gourd contained men, animals, and plants before being split open by lightning
image_query: An ancient stone boat on a misty mountain peak
subject: Assam History
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 72

title: Descent of Khunlung and Khunlai
body: According to Ahom tradition, the heavenly figures Khunlung and Khunlai descended to earth in 568 A.D. by an iron or golden chain, alighting in Mungrimungram. They were sent with sacred items including an idol called Somdeo, a magic sword or Hengdan, two drums, and four cocks for telling omens. Khunlung served as king and Khunlai as chief councillor.
key_facts: Descended from heaven in 568 A.D.
Brought the Somdeo idol and the Hengdan (magic sword)
Khunlung was the elder brother and king; Khunlai was the younger and chief councillor
image_query: Two figures descending from the sky by a chain onto a lush green valley
subject: Assam History
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 74

title: Origin and Identity of the Ahoms
body: The Ahoms are genuine Shans by physical type, tribal language, and written character, originally hailing from the ancient kingdom of Pong (specifically Maulung). They call themselves Tai, meaning 'celestial origin'. Unlike later Shan migrant tribes in Assam such as the Khamtis, Phakials, and Turungs—who are Buddhists—the Ahoms migrated before the inhabitants of their original cradle converted to Buddhism.
key_facts: Original home was in the ancient kingdom of Pong (Maulung)
Identify as Tai, meaning 'celestial origin'
Migrated before their homeland converted to Buddhism, unlike later Shan tribes in Assam

subject: Assam History
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 77

title: Sukapha's Migration to Assam
body: Sukapha, a descendant of the royal line and founder of the Ahom kingdom in Assam, left Maulung in 1215 A.D. He traveled with two elephants, 300 horses, eight nobles, and 9,000 followers. After wandering and raiding in the Patkai hills for thirteen years, he crossed the Khamnamjang river in 1228 A.D. and reached Khamjang and the Nongnyang lake.
key_facts: Left Maulung in 1215 A.D. with 9,000 followers, 8 nobles, 2 elephants, and 300 horses
Stole the Somdeo from the Raja of Mungkang before fleeing
Arrived in Khamjang in 1228 A.D. after thirteen years in the Patkai hills

title: Establishment of Charaideo (1253 A.D.)
body: After years of moving through various flooded tracts along the Brahmaputra, Sukapha abandoned Simaluguri in 1253 A.D. and built a permanent city at Charaideo amid general rejoicings. To celebrate the occasion, two horses were sacrificed to the Gods, and prayers were offered by the Deodhais under a mulberry tree. The neighboring country was at the time inhabited by the Morans (ruled by Badancha) and the Borahis (ruled by Thakumtha).
key_facts: Charaideo was founded and built as a city in 1253 A.D.
Two horses were sacrificed and Deodhais prayed under a mulberry tree to mark the occasion.
The surrounding territory was held by the Moran and Borahi tribes.
image_query: Charaideo maidams
subject: Assam History
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 78

title: Subjugation and Assimilation of Morans and Borahis
body: Sukapha fought and defeated the neighboring Moran and Borahi tribes in turn. Following their defeat, he wisely adopted conciliatory measures, treating them as equals and encouraging intermarriage to weld them all into one nation. He also appointed two great officers of State, the Bar Gohain and the Burha Gohain, who exercised powers second only to the king.
key_facts: Sukapha defeated the Morans and Borahis and united them through equal treatment and intermarriage.
Sukapha appointed two major officers of State: the Bar Gohain and the Burha Gohain.
The Ahoms called Assam Mungdunsunkham, meaning the country full of golden gardens.
image_query: Ancient tribal leaders meeting peacefully in a lush green valley in Assam
subject: Assam History
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 78

title: Reign of Suteupha and Kachari Cession (1268–1281)
body: Sukapha was succeeded by his son Suteupha, who ruled for thirteen years until his death in 1281 A.D. During Suteupha's reign, the Kacharis abandoned the country east of the Dikhu river to the Ahoms. Later, Suteupha sent an expedition against the Naras of Mungkang after they refused a marriage alliance, but his troops were defeated and the commanding Burha Gohain was slain.
key_facts: Suteupha reigned from 1268 to 1281 A.D.
The Kacharis ceded the territory east of the Dikhu river to the Ahoms during his reign.
An expedition against the Naras resulted in a defeat for Ahom forces and the death of the Burha Gohain.
image_query: Medieval Asian treaty signing scroll and old map
subject: Assam History
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 79

title: War with Kamata and Reign of Sukhangpha (1293–1332)
body: Following Subinpha's reign, Sukhangpha ascended the throne in 1293 A.D. Having grown significantly in numbers through natural growth, local recruits, and fresh emigrants, the Ahoms engaged in a succession of wars. They fought a multi-year war against the Raja of Kamata with heavy losses on both sides, which finally concluded when the Kamata ruler sued for peace and gave his daughter Rajani in marriage to the Ahom king.
key_facts: Sukhangpha reigned from 1293 to 1332 A.D.
The Ahoms fought a protracted war against the Raja of Kamata.
Peace was established when the Kamata ruler gave his daughter Rajani in marriage to Sukhangpha.
image_query: Ancient stone fortress gate in a tropical forest
subject: Assam History
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 80

title: Assassination of Sutupha and the Four-Year Interregnum (1364–1380)
body: Sutupha became king in 1364 A.D. amidst frequent disputes with the Chutiyas. In 1376, the Chutiya king visited Sutupha at Chapaguri, invited him to a regatta on the Safrai river under the guise of reconciliation, and treacherously murdered him on his barge. Finding no prince worthy of the throne, the Bar Gohain and Burha Gohain directly ran the administration for a four-year interregnum until raising Tyaokhamti to the throne in 1380.
key_facts: Sutupha was treacherously murdered by the Chutiya king during a regatta on the Safrai river in 1376.
A four-year interregnum from 1376 to 1380 saw the Bar Gohain and Burha Gohain govern the country.
Tyaokhamti was installed as king in 1380 A.D. to end the interregnum.

subject: Assam History
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 81

title: Reign and Origin of Sudangpha (The Brahman Prince)
body: After the nobles assassinated the king in 1389 and ruled without one for some years, a youth named Sudang was discovered in a Habung village and placed on the throne in 1397 at age fifteen. He was the son of Tyaokhamthi's younger queen, who had been set adrift on a raft on the Brahmaputra and rescued by a Brahman. Known as the Brahman Prince, his accession marked the first stage of Hindu and Brahmanical influence among the Ahoms, as he brought his foster-father along to serve as a confidential adviser.
key_facts: Sudangpha ascended the throne in 1397 at age 15.
He was rescued and raised by a Brahman after his mother was set adrift on a raft.
His reign marked the beginning of Brahmanical influence among the Ahoms.
image_query: young prince on a raft on a wide river with a brahmin standing on the shore
subject: Assam History
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 82

title: Origin of the Name Patkai
body: During Sudangpha's reign, Tai Sulai fled to the king of Mungkang for help after a domestic dispute, prompting an invasion. Sudangpha defeated the invaders near Kuhiarbari, and the enemy was pursued up to the Patkai. In 1401, a formal treaty fixed the Patkai as the boundary, with peace negotiated by the two Bar Gohains near the Nongnyang lake. A solemn oath was sworn by cutting up a fowl, from which the word Patkai is said to be derived (Pat-kai-seng-kau meaning cut-fowl-oath-sworn).
key_facts: A treaty in 1401 fixed the Patkai as the boundary between the two countries.
Peace negotiations took place near the Nongnyang lake.
The name Patkai is derived from Pat-kai-seng-kau, meaning cut-fowl-oath-sworn.
image_query: Patkai mountain range landscape
subject: Assam History
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 83

title: Reign of Susenpha and Conflict with the Tangsu Nagas
body: Susenpha, son of Suphakpha, ascended the throne in 1439 and reigned for forty-nine years until 1488. The chief event of his reign was a personal military expedition against the Tangsu Nagas in retaliation for raids, during which the Ahoms lost one hundred and forty men. The minimal references to his long reign in the Buranjis suggest he was a good king under whom the people prospered.
key_facts: Susenpha reigned for 49 years from 1439 to 1488.
He led a personal expedition against the Tangsu Nagas, losing 140 men.
The sparse Buranji records indicate his reign was peaceful and prosperous.
image_query: ancient warriors in a forest skirmish with spears and shields
subject: Assam History
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 84

title: War with the Kacharis and Assassination of Suhenpha
body: In 1490, war broke out between the Ahoms and the Kacharis, resulting in an Ahom defeat at Dampuk on the bank of the Dikhu. The Ahoms sued for peace and sent a princess with a dowry to the Kachari king. Shortly after, in 1493, King Suhenpha was assassinated by Tairungban clan members with a pointed bamboo while repairing the palace, seeking revenge for being punished for paddy theft.
key_facts: The Ahoms were defeated by the Kacharis at Dampuk on the Dikhu river in 1490.
Suhenpha was assassinated in 1493 by members of the Tairungban clan.
The assassins used a pointed bamboo while the king was engaged in palace repairs.

subject: Assam History
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 85

title: Reign of Suhungmung and Annexation of the Chutiya Kingdom
body: Suhungmung, also known as the Dihingia Raja, reigned from 1497 to 1539 and assumed the Hindu title Svarga Narayan, showing the increasing influence of Brahmans. Following prolonged conflicts with the Chutiyas under Dhir Narayan, Suhungmung decisively defeated them in 1523. The Chutiya king and his son were slain, their royal heirlooms were captured, and the entire Chutiya country was annexed to the Ahom kingdom.
key_facts: Suhungmung ruled from 1497 to 1539 and was known as Dihingia Raja.
He assumed the Hindu title Svarga Narayan.
The Chutiya kingdom was annexed in 1523 after a decisive defeat near Sadiya.
A new officer, the Sadiya Khowa Gohain, was appointed to administer the annexed Chutiya territory.

subject: Assam History
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 86

title: Creation of the Barpatra Gohain Office
body: Suhungmung created the new high-ranking appointment of Barpatra Gohain for Senglung, a youth of high-bred appearance who was the son of the late king Supimpha. Although the existing Bar Gohain and Burha Gohain objected and refused to share their men, the king overcame this by assigning the Barahis, Chutiyas, and Morans to the new office. Senglung was then publicly invested and given a seat equal in rank to the other two Gohains.
key_facts: The Barpatra Gohain office was created by Suhungmung for Senglung.
The Bar Gohain and Burha Gohain initially objected to the new appointment.
The new Gohain was given authority over the Barahis, Chutiyas, and Morans.
Senglung's rank was made equal to the Bar Gohain and Burha Gohain.

subject: Assam History
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 89

title: The Rikkhvan Ceremony
body: The Rikkhvan ceremony was an Ahom ritual performed to obtain long life, typically during a king's installation, in times of danger, or following a victory. During the ceremony, tribal priests and astrologers poured holy water purified by sacred texts over the king's seated body. The water ran down through a platform onto the chief astrologer below, after which the king exchanged his clothes and ornaments with the astrologer.
key_facts: Rikkhvan means 'revive life' in Ahom.
The ceremony was performed for longevity during coronations, crises, or after victories.
Deodhai, Mohan, and Bailong priests poured holy water over the king.
The king gave his worn clothes and ornaments to the chief Bailong astrologer.

subject: Assam History
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 88

title: First Recorded Muhammadan Invasion and Defeat
body: In 1527, the first Muhammadan invasion recorded in Ahom history took place under a commander referred to as the great Vazir. The Ahoms successfully attacked his army in front and on both flanks, defeating them and pursuing them as far as the Burai river. During this engagement, they captured forty horses and between twenty and forty cannon.
key_facts: First recorded Muhammadan invasion occurred in 1527.
Ahom forces defeated the invader's army and pursued them to the Burai river.
Captured forty horses and twenty to forty cannon.
image_query: ancient Ahom warriors defending a river fort against invaders
subject: Assam History
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 90

title: Kachari War and Capture of Dimapur
body: In 1531, after a Kachari attack led by Detcha, Suhungmung led a large army up the Dhansiri to punish the Kachari king Khunkhara. The Ahoms captured and burnt Nika, advanced to Dengnut, and eventually forced their way to the Kachari capital at Dimapur on the left bank of the Dhansiri. King Khunkhara fled, and Detsung was installed as the new Kachari ruler after giving his sister in marriage to Suhungmung.
key_facts: Suhungmung led an expedition up the Dhansiri river in 1531.
The Ahom army captured and burnt Nika and advanced to Dimapur.
King Khunkhara fled, and Detsung was installed as a new puppet Kachari prince.

subject: Assam History
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 92

title: Invasion by Turbak and the Naval Battle of Duimunisila
body: In April 1532, a Muhammadan commander named Turbak invaded Assam with a large force of elephants, horses, artillery, and foot soldiers. After initial setbacks for the Ahoms—including a defeat suffered by Suklen—the tide turned in March 1533. A major naval engagement near Duimunisila resulted in a great Ahom victory, where Muhammadan commanders Bangal and Taju were slain alongside massive enemy casualties.
key_facts: Turbak invaded Assam with a large force and artillery in April 1532.
Ahom forces initially suffered reverses under Suklen.
In March 1533, the Ahoms achieved a decisive victory in a naval battle near Duimunisila.

subject: Assam History
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 93

title: Origin of the Morias
body: Following the defeat of the Muslim forces under Turbak, the prisoners of war captured by the Ahoms were settled across the country. Initially ordered to cut grass for the king's elephants and later employed as cultivators, they proved unsuited for these tasks. Left to their own devices, they took up working in brass, leading to their descendants being known as Morias.
key_facts: Muslim prisoners from Turbak's army were settled locally after their defeat.
Unable to perform agricultural or elephant-tending tasks efficiently, they took up brass-working.
Their descendants are known as Morias, continuing the brass-working trade.
image_query: ancient artisan working in brass metalcraft in traditional setting
subject: Assam History
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 95

title: Introduction of Firearms by the Ahoms
body: The use of firearms by the Ahoms dates from the close of the war against Turbak. Up to that conflict, their weapons had consisted strictly of swords, spears, and bows and arrows. Following this campaign, cannon and matchlocks captured from the enemy were integrated into their military capabilities.
key_facts: Ahom weaponry before the war with Turbak was limited to swords, spears, and bows and arrows.
Firearms like cannon and matchlocks were first adopted at the close of this war.
Captured weapons and gunpowder from the conflict helped introduce firearms to Ahom warfare.
image_query: medieval cannon and matchlock firearms in an ancient armory
subject: Assam History
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 94

title: Expeditions against the Nagas (1535–1536)
body: In 1535 and 1536, military operations were launched against the Khamjang, Tablung, and Namsang Nagas under the command of the king's son, Suklen. While the Khamjang Nagas quickly submitted and paid a fine of one hundred mithun (bison), the Tablung and Namsang tribes temporarily inflicted a reverse on the Ahom troops, capturing four guns before eventually making their submission and returning the weapons.
key_facts: Operations against the Khamjang, Tablung, and Namsang Nagas were led by the king's son Suklen.
The Khamjang Nagas surrendered and paid a fine of one hundred mithun.
The Tablung and Namsang Nagas initially defeated the Ahom troops and took four guns, but later returned them and submitted.

subject: Assam History
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 95

title: Final Defeat of Kacharis and Annexation of Dimapur
body: Kachari Raja Detsung renewed hostilities, prompting an Ahom expedition led down to Marangi and the Dhansiri valley. After sustained fighting and the capture of Dimapur, Detsung was pursued, captured at Jangmarang, and put to death in 1536. This campaign resulted in the Ahom annexation of the Dhansiri valley and Kachari possessions north of the Kallang river.
key_facts: Kachari Raja Detsung was defeated and killed at Jangmarang after fleeing Dimapur.
The Ahoms occupied Dimapur twice during the conflict.
The Ahoms gained control of the Dhansiri valley and Kachari territories north of the Kallang river.

subject: Assam History
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 96

title: Assassination of Suhungmung
body: Relations between Suhungmung and his son Suklen became heavily strained over disputes regarding captured Kachari princesses and protocol. In January 1539, Suklen suborned a Kachari servant named Ratiman, who crept into the king's bedroom and stabbed him to death while he slept. Suhungmung thus died after an eventful forty-two-year reign.
key_facts: Suhungmung's reign ended with his assassination in January 1539.
His son Suklen instigated the murder due to growing hostility and personal disputes.
A Kachari servant named Ratiman stabbed the king while he slept in his bedroom.

subject: Assam History
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 97

title: Reign of Suklenmung and First Ahom Coinage
body: Suklenmung succeeded to the throne as a patricide in 1539 and established his capital at Garhgaon, earning the title of the Garhgaya Raja. During his reign, he successfully repelled Koch invasions led by Sukladhvaj (Chilarai) after a decisive victory at the Pichala river. He is notable for being the first Ahom ruler to strike coins, reflecting increased intercourse with civilizations west of Assam. He also excavated the Garhgaon tank, constructed the Naga Ali, and built embankments at Kahikuchi and Changinimukh before dying in 1552.
key_facts: Became king in 1539 and made Garhgaon his capital.
First Ahom ruler to issue coins.
Defeated the Koch forces led by Chilarai at the Pichala river.
Constructed public works including the Garhgaon tank and Naga Ali.

subject: Assam History
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 98

title: Conflict with Koch King Nar Narayan and Chilarai
body: During the reigns of Suklenmung and his successor Sukhampha, the Ahoms engaged in a series of major conflicts with the Koch king Nar Narayan and his generalissimo brother, Sukladhvaj (Chilarai). After initial Ahom successes, Chilarai launched a powerful naval and land invasion up the Brahmaputra in 1562, defeating the Ahoms and occupying Garhgaon. The Ahom king Sukhampka (the Khora Raja) sued for peace through the Burha Gohain, accepting Koch supremacy, territorial cessions, hostages, and a heavy war indemnity.
key_facts: Koch forces led by Chilarai invaded and captured Garhgaon in 1562.
Sukhampka (Khora Raja) fled to Charaikharang in Namrup.
Peace terms included acknowledging Koch supremacy, sending noble hostages, and paying a large indemnity.
Hostages were later released, allowing the Ahoms to recover their lost territories.

subject: Assam History
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 100

title: Release of Ahom Hostages and Return of Artisans
body: In 1564, the Ahom hostages taken by the Koch king Nar Narayan were returned to Assam. While popular tradition attributed this freedom to a successful game of dice won by a hostage against Nar Narayan, Koch Buranjis state it was done after Nar Narayan was defeated by the Gaur Padshah to secure Ahom friendship. Accompanying the returning hostages were Koch artisans, including potters skilled in making images of Durga and other Hindu deities.
key_facts: Ahom hostages were released by the Koch king in 1564.
The release helped the Ahoms easily recover their territories on the north bank.
Koch artisans, including skilled potters, accompanied the returning hostages to Assam.

subject: Assam History
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 101

title: Invasion by the Dhekeri Raja (1563)
body: In January 1563, a Dhekeri Raja invaded Assam accompanied by two rebellious sons of the Ahom Deka Raja (heir-apparent). The invaders were decisively defeated at Murabhaga by the Ahoms, and the Dhekeri Raja fled by boat, abandoning his elephants and weapons. The heads of the slain were piled in heaps at Kahikusi and Narayanpur.
key_facts: Invasion occurred in January 1563
Invaders defeated at Murabhaga by the Ahoms
Heads of the slain piled in heaps at Kahikusi and Narayanpur

title: Nara War and Treaty with Sukhampha (1576)
body: In 1576, the Nara Raja of Mungkang advanced with an army to Khamjang. Hostilities were initially averted when Sukhampha agreed to pay 16,000 rupees in exchange for the Nara Raja's daughter in marriage. However, the Nara Raja sent his sister instead, leading Sukhampha to send men to abduct the daughter. This provoked an invasion of Namrup, where the Nara forces were ultimately vanquished near the Sessa river.
key_facts: Nara Raja of Mungkang invaded Khamjang in 1576
Sukhampha paid 16,000 rupees under a treaty
Nara troops defeated near the Sessa river after an abduction dispute

title: Reign and Death of Sukhampha (1603)
body: Sukhampha reigned for 51 years, a period marked by several plots, harem scandals, and natural disasters including a virulent small-pox epidemic in 1574, a locust swarm in 1569, and a severe earthquake in 1596 that threw up hot water, sand, and ashes while destroying one of his palaces. He died at Khowang in 1603.
key_facts: Sukhampha had a 51-year reign ending in his death in 1603
Major earthquake occurred in 1596, destroying a palace
Experienced a severe small-pox epidemic in 1574 and locusts in 1569

title: Reliability of Ahom Buranjis vs. Later Accounts
body: Edward Gait preferred the chronology of the original Buranjis over later accounts by Kasinath, Robinson, and Gunabhiram for the intermediate Ahom kings. The Buranjis are corroborated by precise dates matching Muhammadan histories and detailed yearly entries, making them more reliable than Kasinath's dates, which were likely skewed by misattRIBUTED coins.
key_facts: Buranjis provide consistent and detailed chronological records
Dates align accurately with Muhammadan histories of 1615, 1637, and 1662
Kasinath's divergent dates for intermediate kings are considered erroneous

subject: Assam History
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 104
